source.title: The Effect of Network Width on Stochastic Gradient Descent and Generalization: an Empirical Study
source.authors: Daniel S. Park; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein; Quoc V. Le; Samuel L. Smith

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how test performance changes with network width, but does not test the memorization threshold or zero-training-error conditions in V2.
record.gate_note: The study reports width-related test-accuracy trends and their dependence on SGD noise scale. It does not report random-label fitting, training error at the relevant widths, or whether the tested widths exceed a zero-training-error threshold. Values in the cited plots are figure-only; rows below record only trends explicitly described in the text.
record.test_reason: The study measures width-dependent test accuracy and optimal SGD noise, but does not establish that its width comparisons are beyond a zero-training-error threshold (V2). Batch-size comparisons use batch-dependent training budgets rather than fixed epochs (V5), and dropout is bundled with other regularizers (V6). Its own results therefore do not test a listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, optimal normalized noise scales proportionally with width without batch normalization; with batch normalization, analogous optimal-learning-rate and batch-size trends hold for WRNs but are weaker for CNNs. Best observed test accuracy increases with width in both families. The authors speculate, without testing larger widths, that stability and minimum-batch constraints could eventually prevent further gains.
record.recipe_differences: Studies width-dependent test performance and SGD noise-scale tuning; it does not use random-label memorization or test performance beyond a zero-training-error threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: The width-related performance pattern depends on SGD noise scale and batch normalization; with batch normalization, WRNs and CNNs behave differently. Parameterization scheme also affects the reported performance comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Best observed test accuracy increases with width, but without batch normalization wider networks do not consistently outperform narrower ones at a fixed suboptimal normalized noise scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width-related accuracy gains depend on tuning SGD noise; this study does not locate those gains relative to interpolation.

fits_no_version.finding: With batch normalization, wider WRNs favor larger learning rates and smaller batches, whereas wider CNNs improve across a broader range of these settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relationship between width, optimal SGD settings and test accuracy depends on architecture and batch normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Combining dropout, label smoothing and augmentation increases final WRN accuracy while preserving the width scaling of optimal normalized noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A combined regularization recipe improves accuracy without eliminating sensitivity to SGD noise.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 97, 2019
record.problems: The supplied text reports many outcomes only in figures, without extractable numerical values. The authors state that their experiments may not probe asymptotic behavior, and that they could not perform additional experiments at larger widths. They do not measure training error or random-label memorization for the width comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The supplied text includes many width-specific figure results, but does not provide their values in extractable text; rows capture the separately described qualitative conditions and trends.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level random-label test accuracy alongside natural-label generalization using the same architectures and recipes.
Test-error behavior beyond the width required for zero training error; neither training-error measurements nor the interpolation threshold are reported.
A controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparison and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and whether recipe changes remove a penalty under that constraint.
The isolated effect of adding dropout, small-data and excessive-dropout regimes, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, training–test gaps and comparisons with alternative generalization measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples compared with equally numerous random removals.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions; the rows' qualitative findings are supported by the text. Batch searches use T = max(Tmin, Emin × Ntrain/B), so epochs are not held fixed throughout. Hyperparameters are selected by test accuracy, and summaries exclude unsuccessful runs. These choices qualify the reported performance comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization on the same architectures and recipes.
Whether networks reach zero training error; whether the widths exceed the width needed for zero training error; the specified one-hidden-layer MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 setting.
A direct convolutional versus fully connected comparison and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and the effects of optimizer tuning or weight decay.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and batch-size adaptation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the training–test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.note: The authors describe this as the WRN trend, similar to the trend without batch normalization.
rows.check: Optimal learning-rate and batch-size trends do not measure post-interpolation generalization or a fixed-epoch batch-size penalty. The dominant-factor interpretation is the authors' explanation.
